stories.headline: Hochul runs on her data center pause and Blakeman's Trump ties as he closes on taxes
stories.summary: A week before Election Day, Gov. Kathy Hochul is making the statewide data center pause she once resisted a centerpiece of her re-election campaign, Gothamist reports, and her final TV ads tie Republican Bruce Blakeman to President Trump. Blakeman, who says Hochul failed to prepare for the industry, is closing with an ad warning that she will raise taxes with Mayor Zohran Mamdani. Early voting in the city is running ahead of 2022, and separately Hochul said her job would be "a lot easier" if Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu loses Israel's election, held today.
stories.why_it_matters: New Yorkers choose a governor on Nov. 3, and early voting is open through Sunday. Both candidates pitch their data center stance as a way to hold down utility bills, and Blakeman has said he would rescind the pause, so the result decides whether it stays.
stories.background: Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul is seeking re-election against Republican Bruce Blakeman. In July she used an executive order to freeze new large data centers statewide for up to a year, the first such statewide pause in the country, after the Legislature passed its own moratorium bill that her office said needed more work. Hochul said the pause gives state agencies time to write rules so data centers pay their share of utility costs and protect the environment. Blakeman opposes a statewide moratorium and says local governments should be able to strike their own deals with tech companies. Siena's public polls have shown Hochul ahead by about 10 points since the summer.

facts.text: Gothamist reports that Hochul once resisted a pause on data centers but that the moratorium is now central to her campaign.
Blakeman says Hochul failed to prepare for the data center industry.
In July, Hochul moved by executive order to impose the country's first statewide moratorium on data centers, lasting up to a year.
Blakeman has criticized the moratorium, said local governments should be able to make data center deals, and said he would rescind the pause.
A Hochul campaign ad in September presented the moratorium as saving New Yorkers money on utility bills and attacked Blakeman for supporting new data centers.
A September Siena poll of likely voters had Hochul ahead of Blakeman by nine points, 50% to 41%, little changed from August.
In the final week, Hochul's campaign is spending millions on TV ads, including three new ones, that tie Blakeman to President Trump, amNY reports.
Blakeman's closing 30-second digital ad claims that after the election Hochul will work with Mayor Zohran Mamdani to raise taxes by billions of dollars, the New York Post reports.
Hochul said Tuesday that Mamdani's supporters likely "aren't thrilled" about the two of them appearing together, and that that was fine, the New York Post reported.
Hochul said her job would be "a lot easier" if Netanyahu loses his election, The Times of Israel reported.
Early voting in New York runs from Oct. 24 through Nov. 1, and Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3.

Early voting turnout has been heavy: amNY says the city's early vote is outpacing the 2022 governor's race, and the Times reported nearly twice as many New Yorkers voted on the first day as four years ago.

framing.note: Frames the data center pause as a turnaround for Hochul that now anchors her campaign, and gives Blakeman's criticism.
Leads with Hochul's attack ads tying Blakeman to Trump, paired with strong early turnout in the city.
Leads with Blakeman's warning that Hochul will raise taxes, and adopts his ad's description of Mamdani's "socialist agenda."
Leads with Hochul's Netanyahu quote for readers following Israel's election, identifying her only as New York's governor.

coverage.takeaway: Headline and summary only: how the data center moratorium became a campaign issue, with Blakeman's criticism.
Headline and summary only: Hochul's final-week ad push against Blakeman and early voting outpacing 2022.
Headline and summary only: Blakeman's closing ad casting Hochul as Mamdani's partner on tax hikes.

stories.headline: GOP challenger Komatireddy runs as a crime fighter against Letitia James
stories.summary: Republican Saritha Komatireddy is running for state attorney general on a law-and-order message against Democratic incumbent Letitia James, and the New York Times reports her long-shot bid has gained momentum and Republican donor support. She has criticized James's comments on the Cornell case, which also came up at a NY1 debate this month. Voters decide on Nov. 3.
stories.why_it_matters: The attorney general is New York's top lawyer, and the race decides whether James keeps the office or a Trump-endorsed former federal prosecutor replaces her. Today's only ingested coverage is from the New York Times (lean left), and it is paywalled.
stories.background: Letitia James, a Democrat, is seeking another term as attorney general and has long been in a legal feud with President Trump. Her Republican challenger, Saritha Komatireddy, is a former federal prosecutor running on a law-and-order platform, and Trump has endorsed her. Komatireddy has criticized James's public comments about the so-called Cornell 7 case, and James was pressed in a NY1 debate on whether she can be impartial in it. A September Siena poll had James ahead by 13 points.

facts.text: The New York Times reports that Komatireddy's long-shot candidacy has gained momentum and support from Republican donors, and that she is running as a crime fighter.
Komatireddy has criticized James's comments on the Cornell case.
Komatireddy is a former federal prosecutor running a law-and-order campaign.
Trump has endorsed Komatireddy against James, with whom he has been in a long-running feud over mortgage fraud allegations.
In a NY1 debate this month, James was pressed on how she could be impartial in the Cornell 7 case given her public statements about it.
A September Siena poll had James leading Komatireddy by 13 points.

coverage.takeaway: Headline and summary only (paywalled): profiles Komatireddy as an underdog whose crime-focused run is gaining donor support.

stories.headline: No A trains between Rockaway Blvd and Lefferts Blvd for nine days starting Nov. 7
stories.summary: The MTA will suspend A train service between Rockaway Blvd and Ozone Park-Lefferts Blvd in Queens for nine straight days starting Nov. 7 while it replaces aging signals on the Liberty Avenue Line. Lefferts-bound trains will run to Howard Beach-JFK Airport instead, and free shuttle buses will cover the gap. The work is part of a larger signal upgrade on the A and C lines announced last week.
stories.why_it_matters: Riders on the Lefferts Blvd branch will need shuttle buses or other routes from Nov. 7 to Nov. 16. The broader project aims to replace old signals on the A and C lines in Brooklyn and Queens with a modern train-control system. Only amNY (center) covered the outage in today's ingest.
stories.background: The Liberty Avenue Line carries the A train's Lefferts Blvd branch through southern Queens. The MTA is replacing signals there and on the Fulton Street line in Brooklyn with communications-based train control. Gov. Kathy Hochul announced the start of the work on Oct. 22, calling it the largest subway signal replacement project in MTA history. The project is paid for with congestion pricing revenue.

facts.text: A trains will not run between Rockaway Blvd and Ozone Park-Lefferts Blvd for nine consecutive days starting Nov. 7 as the MTA replaces aging signals on the Liberty Avenue Line.
The MTA says the suspension runs from 12:30 a.m. Saturday, Nov. 7, to 5 a.m. Monday, Nov. 16.
Trains that normally go to Ozone Park-Lefferts Blvd will be rerouted to Howard Beach-JFK Airport, and free shuttle buses will stop at 104 St and 111 St.
The MTA says crews will replace switches and track near 104 St during the outage.

Hochul announced on Oct. 22 the start of what her office called the largest subway signal replacement project in MTA history, bringing communications-based train control to the A and C lines in Brooklyn and Queens.
The signal work is among subway projects funded by congestion pricing revenue.

coverage.takeaway: Headline and summary only: a service alert with the dates, stations and reason for the outage.

stories.headline: Retired detective indicted in GWB killing as Con Ed workers watch in court
stories.summary: Victor Romero, 62, the retired NYPD detective accused of fatally shooting Con Edison worker Koran Irvine on the George Washington Bridge earlier this month, appeared in Manhattan Criminal Court on Tuesday as Irvine's co-workers looked on. A grand jury indicted him, amNY and the New York Post report, and the Post says the indictment is for murder. At his arraignment last week, where bail was set at $1 million, he pleaded not guilty to manslaughter.
stories.why_it_matters: The case involves a former police officer charged in a road-rage killing of a city utility worker. Irvine's family had questioned why he was first charged with manslaughter rather than murder, and the indictment sets the charges he will face at trial.
stories.background: Koran Irvine, a Con Edison worker, was shot and killed while driving across the George Washington Bridge in what has been described as a road-rage shooting. Victor Romero, a retired NYPD detective, was arrested and arraigned last week on a manslaughter charge, with bail set at $1 million. Prosecutors said in court that the two men's cars nearly collided on the approach to the bridge before Romero fired the shot that killed Irvine. Irvine's family has publicly questioned the manslaughter charge.

facts.text: Romero, 62, appeared in Manhattan Criminal Court on Tuesday, and a grand jury indicted him.
The New York Post reports that Romero was indicted for murder.
Con Edison workers attended the hearing, and amNY and the Daily News described them reacting with pain and anger and confronting Romero.
Bail was set at $1 million at Romero's arraignment last week.
At that arraignment, Romero pleaded not guilty to a manslaughter charge.
Prosecutors said at his arraignment that Romero's and Irvine's cars nearly collided at the approach to the bridge before Romero fired a shot that killed Irvine.
Irvine's family has questioned the manslaughter charge against Romero.

framing.note: Leads with Con Ed workers' grief and anger, keeping the victim's colleagues at the center.
Emphasizes a confrontation between the workers and Romero, and names him as a retired NYPD cop.
Leads with the first courtroom photos of Romero and says he was indicted for murder.

coverage.takeaway: Headline and summary only: courtroom scene told through Con Ed workers, noting the grand jury indictment.
Headline only: frames the hearing as workers confronting Romero.
Headline and summary only: Romero's appearance in court and his indictment for murder.

stories.headline: Police search for man who raped a woman at knifepoint in Central Park
stories.summary: A 39-year-old woman reported being raped at knifepoint on the east side of Central Park on Saturday night, and police have released photos of the man they are looking for. The NYPD says it has stepped up patrols in the park, and no arrest had been reported as of Tuesday. Mayor Zohran Mamdani called the attack "horrific," and The New York Sun says he dodged a question about park safety.
stories.why_it_matters: Central Park is used every day by huge numbers of New Yorkers, and the attacker has not been caught. The attack has also become part of the debate over public safety under Mamdani.
stories.background: The attack happened around 8:30 p.m. on Saturday, Oct. 24, near the park's Fifth Avenue side in the East 60s, police said. The NYPD released photos and video of the suspect, whom it describes as a man in his 30s, on Monday. Central Park has its own NYPD precinct, and the department's figures show slightly more rapes reported there this year than at the same point last year. Mamdani, a democratic socialist, took office as mayor in January, and critics on the right have pressed him on crime.

facts.text: A 39-year-old woman reported being raped at knifepoint in Central Park on Saturday night, near East 66th Street and Fifth Avenue, police said.
Police released photos of the man they are seeking, whom they describe as in his 30s.
Police said they had increased patrols in the park, and the suspect remained at large as of Tuesday.
Mamdani called the attack "horrific" and said the NYPD is investigating.

NYPD figures showed four rapes reported in the Central Park Precinct through Oct. 18, compared with three in the same period last year, PIX11 reported; The New York Sun counts Saturday's attack as the park's fifth rape this year.

framing.note: Leads with the police response, stepped-up patrols, rather than the hunt for the suspect.
Leads with the manhunt and the suspect's released photos.
Makes the mayor the subject, saying he dodged a safety question, and counts this as the park's fifth rape this year.
Casts the attack as a political story about what it calls Democrats' silence, and stresses that it happened in a wealthy area.

coverage.takeaway: Headline and summary only: the police account of when and where the attack happened, with no arrest as of Monday.
Headline and summary only (paywalled): the woman's report and the NYPD's added patrols.
Headline only: the release of photos of the suspect.
Headline only: centers Mamdani's answer to a question about park safety and the year's count of rapes in the park.
Headline and summary only: the NYPD account, framed around what it calls Democrats' silence.

stories.headline: City is slow to put agencies' records requests online, advocates say
stories.summary: The city has been slow to carry out a law requiring every agency to upload public records requests and data to an online portal, THE CITY reports, and good-government advocates say the delay holds back transparency. The City Council passed the bill last November.
stories.why_it_matters: The portal would let any New Yorker see what records people have requested from city agencies and what was released. Only THE CITY (center) covered this in today's ingest.
stories.background: New Yorkers can request records from city agencies under the state Freedom of Information Law, known as FOIL. Last November the City Council passed a bill, Intro 1235, sponsored by Council Member Gale Brewer, requiring city agencies to publicly report their FOIL requests through an online portal. Good-government groups testified to the Council in March and June about how the city is carrying out the law.

facts.text: THE CITY reports the city is moving slowly on a requirement that all agencies upload records requests and data to an online public portal, which good-government advocates say delays transparency.
The City Council passed the bill last November.
Intro 1235 of 2025, sponsored by Council Member Gale Brewer, requires city agencies to publicly report their FOIL logs.
Good-government groups gave joint testimony to the City Council on implementing the city's FOIL law in March and again in June 2026.

coverage.takeaway: Headline and summary only: THE CITY's own reporting on the delayed rollout, with advocates' criticism.
